newsitem.title: UK: Reform in South America creates scope for shipping.
newsitem.headline: Reform in South America creates scope for shipping.

text.p: Economic reform and political stability are opening up opportunities for shipping companies to expand in South America, according to a new report.
However, the report by Drewry Shipping Consultants says questions remain about which ports will gain regional supremacy.

The report argues that economic reforms have led to increasing prosperity which is "providing considerable opportunities for those looking to enter or expand their shipping connections with the region."

These opportunities are particularly open to international operators as the report, "South American Shipping: From Crisis and Chaos to Stability and Prosperity", says countries in the region own just 2.1 percent of the world fleet in deadweight terms.

The six leading South American economies, Brazil, Argentina, Venezuela, Chile, Colombia and Peru, collectively generate exports worth up to $125 billion and import goods worth roughly the same amount. However, Drewry points out that in 1990 collective imports totalled just $46.8 billion.
But Drewry warns that if imports continue to expand as quickly they could imbalance economies and transport movements, particularly of consumer goods in containers on north-south services.
Development of the Mercosur free trade association is encouraging coastal movements between Argentina and Brazil where the main competitive west coast ports are based.

"The battle ground looks likely to centre on hubbing -- which ports are to be the focus for the turnrounds of the main haul services and, therefore, the centres for regional feeding operations," the report says.
Concern has long centred on the inefficiency of older central hub ports such as Santos in Brazil to services running from Europe or North America and turning round in South America.
Congestion, labour problems and ageing equipment which delay ships cause problems to services run to fixed timetables.
Increasing port privatisation is slowly beginning to answer the problem, though.
Drewry points to new contenders in Brazil such as the growing private ports of Sepetiba and Rio Grande, as well as reform at Santos.
It adds that Buenos Aires and Montevideo in Argentina may also be in the frame as turning ports on the east coast. Buenos Aires has benefited from the success of a new privately-owned terminal.
In the west it says various Chilean ports will be vying with Callao in Peru and Guayaquil in Ecuador.
